How the kernel scheduler works

By Ada Example

The scheduler picks the next task to run on each CPU. It has to be fair to every task, quick to decide, and careful with caches, all at once. This post walks through how it balances those demands, and what changed in the latest release.

Each CPU keeps its own queue of runnable tasks. Since the latest release, that queue is a lock-free run queue, so waking a task on another CPU no longer takes a lock that every other CPU also wants. See the about page for who we are.

Fairness comes from tracking how much CPU time each task has had, weighted by its priority. The task that has had the least runs next. This keeps interactive programs responsive even when a long build keeps every core busy for minutes on end.

Load balancing moves tasks between queues when one CPU is much busier than another. It runs rarely, because moving a task loses whatever it had in the old CPU's caches, and that cost often outweighs the gain from a shorter queue.
